newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Norfolk Southern set back in Conrail case.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norfolk Southern set back in Conrail case.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp. suffered major setbacks Thursday on two fronts in its attempt to wrest Conrail Inc. from an intended merger with CSX Corp..

A federal judge in Philadelphia and the Surface Transportation Board in Washington each rejected separate requests by Norfolk Southern to invalidate a provision in the merger agreement by Conrail and CSX not to discuss a deal with another party until 1999.
The rulings, if upheld in appeals promised by Norfolk Southern, mean Conrail could not consider Norfolk Southern's $10.3 billion bid for the Philadelphia-based railroad for two years.

The decisions, if they stand, increase the prospect that Conrail shareholders will cast a crucial vote in favor of the CSX merger at a company meeting next week, analysts and Conrail representatives said.
"They (CSX) have't done it yet, but they have solidified their position and they have further made Norfolk Southern an underdog," said Anthony Hatch, an analyst for brokerage Natwest Securities Corp.

Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern had argued the two-year "lockout" or "no-shop" provision would unfairly prevent Conrail shareholders from seriously weighing its rival offer when voting on Jan. 17 on a major provision of the CSX-Conrail merger, which is worth about $9.1 billion at Thursday's stock prices.

The U.S. District Court in Philadelphia also rejected a request by Norfolk Southern and a group of Conrail shareholders to order Richmond, Va.-based CSX to pay $110 per share cash for all of Conrail, rather than for only a 40 percent stake, as CSX has proposed.
CSX intends to swap common and preferred stock for the remaining 60 percent.

That Norfolk Southern request was based on a Pennsylvania anti-takeover law requiring a company or group that has acquired a stake of 20 percent or more in another company to pay "fair value," or equivalent terms, for all remaining shares.
Norfolk Southern argued CSX had exceeded the 20 percent threshold because shares held by Conrail's directors should be counted along with a 19.9 percent stake CSX bought in a tender offer.
But in his ruling, U.S. District Judge Donald Van Artsdalen said any exceeding of the threshold was "clearly inadvertent."
CSX last week sold 85,000 Conrail shares, thus bringing the stake below 20 percent even if Conrail board member holdings were counted.

In addition, Van Artsdalen refused Norfolk Southern's request to block next week's Conrail shareholders meeting -- which will vote on waiving the Pennsylvania law for the CSX-Conrail merger -- until a final legal decision could be reached on the "fair value" challenge.
He said it was unlikely Norfolk Southern would ultimately succeed in the challenge.

In ruling on the two-year lockout, which was adopted in December when CSX raised its bid for Conrail, Van Artsdalen noted he had already upheld a 270-day lockout in a previous merger agreement between the two railroads.
"I see no principled reason as to why the lockout could not be extended (to 1999)," he said. Van Artsdalen issued his rulings after a four-hour court hearing Thursday.

The Surface Transportation Board said in its decision the lockout "appears excessive on its face," but said it was premature to rule on the issue. It said it retained the authority to invalidate the lockout if it approved what Norfolk Southern has said will be a rival proposal it will make to the board to merge with Conrail.
A Conrail spokeswoman said even in that case, a merger with Norfolk Southern would require the approval of Conrail's board and shareholders.
Norfolk Southern immediately said it would appeal the judge's rulings. In a statement, it also urged Conrail shareholders to vote against the waiver on Jan. 17.

"They can send a clear message to Conrail's board that CSX's latest bid is unacceptable and that shareholders want the opportunity to consider Norfolk Southern's superior all-cash offer of $115 per share --- an offer worth over $1 billion more than CSX's," Norfolk Southern said.
Conrail spokesman Rudy Husband welcomed the court rulings, and said they increased the likelihood Conrail shareholders would allow the merger with CSX to proceed.
"This decision certainly enhances the prospects of us being successful on January 17," Husband said.
CSX Chairman John Snow, who testifed at Thursday's court hearing, said Van Artsdalen's ruling, assuming it is upheld, "reduces a lot of uncertainty."
